div.head: Chapter 17
div.p: The second reason for this can be framed as follows. That government is unjust, tyrannical, and abominable that places all its subjects — great and small alike, men and women, young and old, natural lords and their subjects and servants — indiscriminately in most harsh, bitter, and perpetual servitude, and in all the vile labors and services that present themselves to those who oppress them. Now these encomiendas and repartimientos are of this kind and produce what has been described. Therefore they are tyrannical, and such a manner of governing is tyrannical and most iniquitous.

The minor premise is well clear from what has been recounted above, and is visible today in the province of Nicaragua and the others we mentioned: where not a creature remains from the time it can stand on its own feet that does not serve.

The third reason says thus: that manner of governing free men is tyrannical, unjust, and impious that deprives of their states, dignity, jurisdiction, and dominions, and of their vassals and subjects, those who are the true and legitimate lords by natural law and the law of nations. This is manifest as regards the law, because if to deprive a private person of his cloak is tyrannical and impious, how much more so to deprive lords and kings of their kingdoms and dominions. Now through the said repartimientos kings and lords are deprived of their states and their subjects, etc.
Therefore such a manner of governing is tyrannical, most iniquitous, and impious.

The minor premise as regards the fact is no less manifest from what has been said, and the whole world knows that the natural lords have no freedom over their own peoples, since all their subjects have been distributed among the Spaniards, and the lords themselves also serve and pay tribute, and as has been said, they are the most oppressed and afflicted when their subjects fail to pay the tyrannical tributes that the Spaniards have imposed upon them. I will not speak of the innumerable natural kings and lords who have perished under this Pharaonic servitude, and the immediate successors of those who live under it today, dying in extreme misery. Therefore unjust and tyrannical and abominable is the governance that is and has always been exercised through those repartimientos.

The fourth reason: that manner of ruling and governing free men is tyrannical and iniquitous that is not ordered toward the good and benefit and growth of those who are to be governed, but toward the private good of those who govern. This is a maxim of all the moral philosophers — Aristotle, book 3 of the Politics and book 8 of the Ethics — and of all the theologians; and of this no one of sound mind doubts. Now that which exists today, and has always existed in the Indies from the year 1505 when this plague of repartimientos began, is precisely this. Therefore it is tyrannical, and worse than iniquitous.

The minor is proved by everything that has been said, and setting aside what all those who have been and seen in those parts report: namely, the insatiable greed and ambition of those who have held repartimientos, on account of which everything they have thought, said, and done in those lands has been directed and ordered toward their own temporal interest, and to the harm and ruin of the Indians; for they have made no more account of them, in terms of their use of them, than they do of their animals, and I could swear that many have cared for and tended their pack animals far more than they have the Indians. For they do not load the animals with a greater burden than they can carry, and they give them sufficient food; but upon the Indians they have loaded and do load today insupportable burdens without giving them anything to eat. They tend their animals when they are sick, but the Indians they have not cared for nor can they bear the sight of them beyond the point where they fall ill; and then they send them without remedy or relief and without food back to their lands, which are commonly forty or fifty or more leagues away. They have taken from them their entire order of governance, which was far better for those without the light of faith than our own, and have given them none that is any good, but the same they give their livestock or animals. And so, setting aside what all those who have been there and seen it know, this reason should suffice for those on that side and those on this side, and for men throughout the whole world, even those who are more than barbarians, as the most manifest proof that such governance has been and is not ordered toward the good and benefit of those peoples, but toward their pernicious and total destruction; and that the Spaniards have not cared for them nor had any regard for them beyond their use for becoming rich; for under these repartimientos and through their use, more than thirty million souls have perished, the greater part without faith and without sacraments, and more than four thousand leagues of land that were most densely populated have been depopulated, and we now see them empty. I could recount here wonders that would astonish the world of the particular harms the Indians have received from the Spaniards through these repartimientos.

The fifth reason can be framed thus: that regime or governance is tyrannical and iniquitous and worthy of all fire and torment by which men are consumed and utterly perish and kingdoms and provinces are depopulated.

That this is precisely what the Spaniards have imposed in the Indies is plainly contrary to the just governance and manner and care of ruling free men; and even were they not free, the one who governs must always keep before his eyes that his duty consists in vigilance over three things that preserve the common good and health of kingdoms, against the three impediments that tend to destroy that common good. The first is that the ruler take the greatest care for the multiplication and succession of men in the towns. The second, that through his laws, rewards, and penalties he make his subjects as virtuous as he can, not permitting them to do injustice or harm to one another. The third, that he defend such subjects from external enemies. On this, Saint Thomas, book 1, chapter 15, and book 3, chapter 3, De regimine principum. And so, by contrast, the Spaniards in the Indies have had no other care than to undo, diminish, and consume those peoples; and to this end they have awaited neither law nor reason nor justice; and thus the Indians have not been defended from their foremost and external enemies — who are the Spaniards themselves, though they may now be called internal since they call themselves encomenderos. Therefore such a manner of governance is most iniquitous, tyrannical, and most cruel, and worthy of all fire.

Let another reason be the sixth: that manner of governing free men is tyrannical, abominable, impious, and most worthy of all hellfire by which unbelievers come to regard the faith with suspicion and judge the Christian religion to be unjust and false and consider it most worthy of being hated and rejected; and those who have already received it are impeded from divine worship, from the teaching of the Church, and from the communication and practice of the holy sacraments. That such encomiendas and repartimientos are of this kind was proved in § 13. We could add there many notable examples of how those who are still unbelievers do not wish to become Christians on account of the sufferings and oppressions they endure and the importunate and excessive tributes, abhorring the faith and regarding the Christian religion as tyrannical; and those who have received it say: "We were well enough before, and would to God these Christians had never come here." So much so that many good religious men who devote themselves to preaching believe or suspect that many of those who have converted have fallen back into idolatry and abandoned the faith, as if it were the mark of a religion false, harsh, and intolerable. Others of us believe that there are those who hold it and would hold it more firmly fixed, and would be improved in their customs day by day, were it not that the excessive tributes and the constant and importunate services leave them no space to hear the doctrine and receive the holy sacraments, and to devote themselves to divine worship and practice other Christian works.

I speak the truth here: that once, passing through a Franciscan monastery in New Spain, the guardian told me that they had confessed that Lent nineteen women whose husbands had gone two years earlier in search of tribute and had not returned. Of these there are each day many who, unable to bear such intolerable burdens, flee to the forests in despair, where jaguars eat them, leaving their wives and children abandoned; and countless others for this same reason have hanged themselves.

Unjust then it is, tyrannical, dreadful, and abominable, and worse than any barbarous nation could have devised, such a manner of governing as the Spaniards have imposed in the Indies; and consequently the entire seventh principle appears proved; namely, that their entry and their subsequent conduct in that world and in every part of it has been violent, abominable, tyrannical, and most cruel, and that of cruel enemies, etc.
